theme: Sabbath year, Jubilee, blessings and curses
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 25:1-26:46. The first chapter describes a Sabbath year and a Jubilee, which are among the most radical ideas in the law. The second sets out the blessings and curses of the covenant. Read them together and notice how the second grows out of the first.
settingTheScene: Israel was about to enter a land that God was giving them. Leviticus 25 and 26 explain how they were to live in it. The land belongs to God, and the people are his tenants. Every seventh year, the land was to rest. Every fiftieth year, the Jubilee, property returned to its original family and slaves went free. Chapter 26 then sets out what will happen if Israel obeys and if it does not. It is the close of the Holiness Code and the covenant section of Leviticus.
observation: “When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall keep a Sabbath to the LORD” (25:2).
In the seventh year, the land is not to be sown or harvested, and God promises to provide enough in the sixth year (25:3-22).
The Jubilee is announced on the Day of Atonement: “And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants” (25:9-10).
“The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (25:23).
A relative may “redeem” land or a person who has been sold because of poverty (25:25-28, 47-49).
Israelites are not to be treated as slaves, because “they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt” (25:42).
Obedience will bring rain, harvest, peace, and God’s presence: “I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people” (26:3-13).
Disobedience will lead to escalating discipline, ending in exile, and yet “I will remember my covenant with Jacob” (26:14-45).
interpretation:
The Sabbath year and Jubilee are a vision of a society shaped by grace. The central claim is in 25:23: “The land is mine.” Because God owns the land, no one can own it permanently. The Jubilee resets everything. Debts are cleared, land returns to the families who first received it, and slaves go free. It is a built-in safeguard against the growth of permanent poverty and inequality. No family could be locked out forever.

The reason behind this is the exodus. “They are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt.” Because God redeemed Israel from slavery, Israelites are not to enslave each other. The memory of redemption shapes the economy.

The idea of a redeemer is also introduced here. A relative could buy back land or free a family member who had fallen into debt. This is the background for the story of Ruth and Boaz, and for the later use of the word redeemer for God himself. The redeemer is the one who pays the price to bring back what was lost.

Chapter 26 is the covenant’s summary. It is a promise of blessing for faithfulness and a warning of discipline for rebellion. The blessing is rich: rain, harvest, safety, and God walking among them. But the curses are sobering: disease, defeat, famine, and finally exile. The warnings come in stages, with the repeated phrase “if you will not listen to me.” God does not strike quickly. He disciplines and warns again, and gives space to turn.

The ending of chapter 26 is the most hopeful part. Even in exile, “I will remember my covenant.” God says that he will not “break my covenant with them” (26:44). The covenant ends not with judgment but with a promise. This is the hope the prophets will cling to when the curses fall.
connection: Jesus began his ministry by reading from Isaiah 61, “to proclaim liberty to the captives… to proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor” (Luke 4:18-19), which echoes the Jubilee. He is the true Redeemer, who bought us back from slavery to sin (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 1:18-19). Paul says that the whole creation “will be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:21). Hebrews 4:9 says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.
application:
Consider the claim that everything you have belongs to God. Does that change how you hold your money, your home, or your plans?

Think about people who are trapped in debt or poverty. Is there a way you can act as a redeemer for someone in your life?

Rest in the promise that God remembers his covenant, even when you have failed.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you are holding too tightly, and ask him to teach you to hold it loosely.
Thank him for the Jubilee Christ has brought.
Thank him for remembering his covenant with you.
